newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - "Mr Clean" hopes to sweep Philippine politics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - "Mr Clean" hopes to sweep Philippine politics.

text.p: Philippine Defence Secretary Renato de Villa is banking on his "Mr Clean" image to propel him to the presidency of a nation where corruption is so rife that government officials say they are often perceived as thieves.
If and when the former soldier, who says honour is his personal code, assumes the Philippines' top job, he says he will try to restore morality in public office.
"I think there's nothing wrong with maintaining that virtue if I go into politics," de Villa told Reuters in a recent interview.
"It is something worth introducing back in segments of our population or in our practices, where it may have been lost."
Government corruption is taken for granted in the Philippines and many Filipinos are sceptical of de Villa's vow, having heard similar pledges by other public figures before.
Graft is so endemic in Philippine society that officials estimate the government has lost $48 billion due to corruption during the past 20 years.
CORRUPTION HAS BECOME A 'NIGHTMARE'

In a popular illegal numbers game called "jueteng," gambling syndicates collect up to 60 million pesos ($2.3 million) in bets every day and pay a third of that amount, or 18 million pesos ($690,000) to officials and police as bribes.
President Fidel Ramos has acknowledged corruption in public service had become a "nightmare".

Public cynicism has grown so great that "government transactions are almost always believed to be dishonest, government officials are almost always believed to be rich with ill-gotten wealth," Ramos said in a speech last month.
But what gives de Villa's pledge extra weight is that it comes from a man whose name has never been sullied by scandal in four decades as a soldier and public official, his aides say.

A career soldier who rose from second lieutenant to five-star general, 61-year-old de Villa is one of more than a dozen men and women who either have openly declared presidential aspirations or are perceived as potential successors to President Fidel Ramos.
COY ON PRESIDENTIAL AMBITIONS
De Villa, often described as reticent and aloof, has not stated outright that he will run, but in an interview with Reuters he gave the clearest sign yet of his intentions.

"I have not officially declared that I am running...but all of the plans and all of the actions that we're doing right now are in that direction, and in due time we should be able to arrive at that decision," he said.

De Villa's emergence as a possible presidential candidate coincided with a nationwide controversy over proposals to amend the constitution and allow Ramos to stand for re-election when his current term ends in June 1998.

Despite Ramos's public pledges to step down next year, speculation that he might still be in power into the 21st century has been bolstered by comments from some of his aides, who have said they want the constitution changed to allow Ramos to stand again.
De Villa says he believes Ramos is sincere and that the uproar over possible constitutional changes will eventually die down.

"The president has stated in categorical terms many, many times (that he will not run). Why do we keep asking the same question?" he said, sounding annoyed that anyone should doubt the sincerity of his boss.
A "RAMOS CLONE"?
De Villa has been such a loyal aide to Ramos and is seen to have such a similar leadership style that he is often referred to by the media as a "Ramos clone".
The label does not bother him because it comes from people who do not really know him, he says.
A former armed forces chief before he assumed the defence post in 1991, de Villa helped then defence chief Ramos put down six army coup attempts against Corazon Aquino.
It was also while he was armed forces chief and later defence secretary that the military tamed a 28-year communist insurgency.
He compares the Marxist insurgency to a virus that thrives in conditions of poverty and social injustice. Only when those conditions are wiped out will the virus die, he says.
He ruled out any further military adventurism "in our time", and said the armed forces now respects the constitution.
De Villa says he will announce in the second quarter of this year whether or not he will run for president.
"This is one occasion (in which) I would not want to shoot from the hips," he said. "I would rather take a careful aim to make sure that I don't miss the target."
